title: Getting ready
hookLine: Socrates' last words were about a rooster: why, of all things?
tomorrow: what did a servant know about dying that the doctors didn't?

cards: Some people keep a note on their phone called if anything happens: passwords, who takes the dog, which song to play. It feels morbid to write, and strangely calm once it's done.
Here are some old last words with a strange line in them. In Plato's dialogue the Phaedo, Socrates has drunk the poison. The cold is moving up from his feet, and his face is covered.
Then he uncovers it and says his last words: Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius. Pay it, and don't forget. Of everything a dying man could say, why a rooster?

teach.b: Readers hear it two ways. Asclepius was the god of healing, so some hear thanks, as if death were the cure. Others hear it plainly: a real debt, and Socrates wasn't leaving one unpaid.
Either way, look at the rest of his last day. Plato says he bathed first, so the women wouldn't have the trouble of washing his body.

teach.h: A BATH, THE CHILDREN, THE FRIENDS.
teach.b: He saw his children and sent them home. He talked with his friends until the end.
And earlier that day he told them why he was calm: those who practice philosophy rightly, he said, are practicing dying. In Greek, melete thanatou, the practice of death.
For Plato's Socrates, that practice means loosening the soul's hold on the body's wants and fears, a little every day, so death doesn't arrive as a stranger.
This path borrows the shape: getting ready isn't a job for the last hour.

Done along the way, it leaves almost nothing to settle on the last day. Just a rooster. The plain versions now are a written wish, a thank-you said, an apology made, a note that says where things are.
Not because the end is near, but because a prepared life travels light.

how: Readers of Plato's Phaedo treat getting ready as a lifelong practice: a written wish, debts paid, thanks and apologies said early, so little is left to settle at the end.

o: warming up before a race or a big exam
settling what you owe so the end leaves nothing undone
packing for a long trip you're nervous about taking

games.q: the last day of Socrates: tap the pairs.
p: settled a debt with his last words
the friend asked to pay it
the god of healing, owed a rooster

s: Socrates' last words were about a rooster he owed
Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius; pay it. readers hear it as thanks or as a plain debt.
Socrates spent his last day refusing to talk about death
he talked with his friends about it calmly, until the end.
getting ready for death is only for the very old or very sick
the popular view. Plato's Socrates calls a whole life of philosophy practice for dying.

games.q: your aunt won't write a will: she says it invites bad luck. what fits the shape of the Phaedo?
o: getting ready is a lifelong practice; settling things early makes life lighter.
she's right to wait: Socrates only got ready once the poison was poured.
skip the will: for Socrates only the soul matters, never the paperwork.
games.why: in the Phaedo, Socrates says those who rightly practice philosophy are practicing dying all along. even his last words settled a debt.

practice: With a pen or your phone, write one line you'd want someone to have if anything happened: a wish, a thank-you, or where to find something. Then rest your hand and breathe with that line for the rest of the sit.
You don't have to send it; it only has to be written.

wordCard.voice: Getting ready: for Plato's Socrates, a lifelong practice of dying, so that at the end nothing is left owed. Not even a rooster.

orig.note: Greek: practice of death. Plato's Socrates, in the Phaedo, on what philosophy is.

carryVoice: Keep this one: prepared. By the end, Socrates had only a rooster left to settle. Four of seven, and see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Plato, Phaedo 115a-118a (the bath, the children, the poison, the last words about the rooster owed to Asclepius)
Plato, Phaedo 67e and 81a (those who rightly practice philosophy are practicing dying; melete thanatou)
